t: Minimum Time to Eat All Grains — Binary Search on Time + Greedy Coverage
o: Hens and grains sit on a line; hens move simultaneously at 1 unit/sec; find the minimum T so every grain gets eaten. Each hen will eat a contiguous block of grains (in sorted order), so the question is how to partition the sorted grains among sorted hens. Example 1: hen at 3 takes grain 2 (1s), hen at 6 takes grain 4 (2s), hen at 7 takes 7 and 9 (2s) → T = 2. With n, m up to 2·10⁴, binary searching T with an O(n+m) greedy feasibility check is ideal.
k: A hen at h covering grain interval [g₀, g₁] needs (g₁−g₀) + min(|h−g₀|, |h−g₁|) seconds.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search on T with greedy interval coverage
a.i: Feasibility is monotone in T. To check a given T, sweep hens left to right and assign each hen a maximal prefix of the remaining grains it can finish within T. If grains lie left of the hen, it goes left first then right as far as possible: rightmost reach = h + max(T−d, ⌊(T−d)/2⌋) where d = h − g₀ (left-first or right-first routing, whichever reaches farther). If grains lie right of the hen, reach = h + T provided the nearest grain is within T. If all grains get consumed, T works.
s: check(T): pointer gi over grains; for each hen, compute its rightmost reachable grain given the nearest uncovered grain, advance gi past all covered grains.
a.t: O((n + m) log(maxPos)) — about 31 binary-search iterations, each a linear greedy sweep.
a.sp: O(1) — sorting in place, only pointers.

w: This is the only approach you need: monotone feasibility + greedy contiguous assignment. The subtle part is the mixed-direction reach formula (T−d) vs ⌊(T−d)/2⌋ — going left first lets the hen travel further right than alternating would suggest incorrectly; derive it as: left distance d plus right distance R with d + R ≤ T, or R + (R + d) ≤ T. Pitfalls: forgetting to sort, integer overflow in C++/Java (use long for positions/T), and assuming each hen eats at most one grain. Follow-ups: hens with different speeds, or grains with eating times.
